scenes.title: Were the first galaxies already rich in oxygen?
scenes.narration: At redshift nine to ten, very early in cosmic history, had galaxies already made as much oxygen as nearby galaxies? Five unlensed, directly measured galaxies provide a cleaner clue.
scenes.visual: Series title card; question as the dominant text. NO cover page.

scenes.title: A chemical clock for young galaxies
scenes.narration: Stars forge oxygen and return it to a galaxy's gas, so oxygen abundance acts like a clock. Nearby galaxies define a benchmark at each stellar mass. This paper asks whether galaxies at redshift nine to ten fall clearly below that benchmark.

scenes.title: Lensing and an extrapolated benchmark can mislead
scenes.narration: Two traps can fake a deficit. Gravitational lensing can magnify glowing gas differently from the starlight used to estimate mass. And the usual local benchmark is extrapolated below the masses where it was actually measured. Both must be removed first.

cards.label: benchmark used below its calibrated range

scenes.title: Five strictly unlensed galaxies, directly measured
scenes.narration: The evidence is five strictly unlensed field galaxies from the Pollock CAPERS and JADES sample, redshift nine point three to nine point nine. Their oxygen abundances come from direct electron-temperature measurements, all placed on one consistent scale.

scenes.claim: The five unlensed galaxies average −0.69 ± 0.03 dex below the local mass–metallicity relation — about one fifth today's oxygen level (leave-one-out spread 0.04 dex).
scenes.axis_caption: Across: galaxy stellar mass. Up: gas oxygen abundance. Red circles: the five unlensed galaxies. Curves: the local benchmark.
scenes.title: Every red point sits well below the local relation
scenes.narration: This is the paper's key figure. Across: stellar mass. Up: gas oxygen abundance. Each red circle is one unlensed galaxy — and every one sits below the local relation, averaging zero point six nine dex lower, about one fifth of today's oxygen level.
scenes.overlay_emphasis: red points + vertical gap to local curve

scenes.claim: Swapping the extrapolated Curti et al. (2020) benchmark for the Andrews & Martini (2013) relation measured at these masses changes the deficit by only 0.04 dex, to about −0.65 dex.
scenes.axis_caption: Same figure — now compare the two benchmark curves: extrapolated versus measured at these masses.
scenes.title: Two different benchmarks, nearly the same answer
scenes.narration: Could the benchmark itself be the problem? The figure carries two: one extrapolated, one measured at exactly these masses. Swapping them moves the deficit only from minus zero point six nine to about minus zero point six five dex. The result survives.

scenes.claim: An independent ~1500-galaxy stacked-Te JADES measurement (z = 4–10, 12+log O/H = 7.62 ± 0.10 at log M★ = 8) shows a consistent −0.5 to −0.6 dex normalization deficit.
scenes.axis_caption: Same figure — the blue square is a stack of roughly 1500 galaxies, a fully independent cross-check.
scenes.title: Fifteen hundred stacked galaxies agree
scenes.narration: The blue square is an independent cross-check: roughly fifteen hundred unlensed galaxies, stacked, across redshift four to ten. Their combined measurement lands zero point five to zero point six dex low — the same shortfall, reached by a completely different method.

scenes.title: GN-z11 extends the check; the direction holds
scenes.narration: The famous galaxy G N z eleven, at redshift ten point six, extends the test with larger uncertainty and agrees in direction. Individual galaxies, the stack, and both benchmarks point the same way: a population deficit of minus zero point six four to zero point six eight dex.

cards.label: points, stack, and both anchors agree

scenes.title: Robust direction, uncertain size, no detection claim
scenes.narration: The absolute temperature-based abundance scale remains uncertain by zero point one to zero point two dex.
